analysis.one_liner: Forces faster prosecution of savings and loan fraud and recovery of stolen money.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill with 108 cosponsors to speed up savings and loan fraud prosecutions died in a House subcommittee after one hearing, never getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: During the savings and loan crisis, the Justice Department had more than 21,000 fraud and embezzlement referrals sitting untouched, including 234 involving losses of $1 million or more. This bill ordered the Attorney General to act on half of the backlog by January 1991 and the rest by January 1992, to recover or win restitution for the stolen amounts, and to report to Congress every quarter on progress. The bill died in subcommittee after a single hearing.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who were footing the multi-billion-dollar bill for failed thrifts through the deposit insurance fund; honest depositors; and small savers whose money depended on the system's integrity.

how_it_helps.text: As of February 1990, the FBI had received over 21,000 savings and loan fraud referrals and complaints on which it had taken no action, including 234 involving potential losses of $1 million or more; the bill required action on the backlog within fixed deadlines.

The Attorney General had approved only 47% of the additional FBI agents and 51% of the prosecutors the FBI requested for savings and loan cases, and had requested only $50 million of the $75 million per year Congress authorized for enforcement; the bill pressed the Department to use that capacity.

The bill directed the Attorney General to recover or obtain restitution for amounts lost to savings association fraud or embezzlement, money that otherwise comes out of the taxpayer-backed deposit insurance fund.

It required the Attorney General to testify before the House and Senate Banking Committees every quarter on the status of investigations, prosecutions, and recoveries, creating ongoing public accountability.

analysis.who_pays: Fraud perpetrators and thrift executives who would face accelerated investigation, prosecution, and restitution demands; the Justice Department, which would have had to redirect resources and submit to quarterly oversight; other enforcement priorities would have competed for the same resources.
analysis.who_pays_short: S&L fraud suspects and the Justice Department

drawbacks.text: The bill set rigid deadlines — half of all pending referrals investigated or prosecuted within about six months of enactment, the rest within 18 months — which prosecutors could meet by moving easy cases or stretching thin evidence, rather than by improving case quality.

It did not itself appropriate money; it relied on the Attorney General acting within existing resources, so the mandate could have crowded out other criminal enforcement, from drug cases to organized crime, without new funding to cover it.

It put Congress directly in charge of reviewing individual prosecution progress through quarterly testimony, which critics would call an intrusion on the Justice Department's independence over which cases to pursue.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit was potentially very large: recovering a share of the billions lost to thrift fraud and holding perpetrators accountable, funded with money Congress had already authorized. The main costs were pressure on prosecutorial priorities and some risk of rushed cases. On balance the bill was a modest, oversight-focused response to a documented 21,000-case backlog, and its main weakness was that it forced speed rather than adding resources.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees, referred to subcommittees, got one hearing in July 1990, and then sat there until the Congress ended in January 1991, with no vote ever scheduled.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 7, 1990 with 108 cosponsors from both parties and referred jointly to the Judiciary and Banking committees.
It was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Criminal Justice and the Banking Subcommittee on Financial Institutions Supervision, Regulation and Insurance within days of introduction.
The subcommittees held one hearing on July 11, 1990; the bill was never reported out of committee, never reached the House floor, and died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People and institutions under investigation for savings and loan fraud benefited from the absence of a fixed enforcement deadline, and the Justice Department avoided quarterly public reporting on its handling of the fraud backlog.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: S&L fraud suspects; no new DOJ deadline

for.name: Rep. Stephen L. Neal
for.role: Sponsor, House Democrat from North Carolina
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and marshaled 108 bipartisan cosponsors to force DOJ action on the savings and loan fraud backlog.

for.name: 21 of 175 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Rep. M. Roukema and Rep. W. McCandless.

for.name: House Criminal Justice and Financial Institutions Subcommittees
for.role: Subcommittees of the Judiciary and Banking committees
for.what_they_did: Held a joint-stage hearing on the bill on July 11, 1990.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Committee that never advanced the bill to markup or the floor
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to subcommittee and took no further action after the July 1990 hearing; the bill never left committee for a floor vote.

against.name: Attorney General Richard Thornburgh
against.role: Head of the Department of Justice
against.what_they_did: The bill was written in response to the Justice Department requesting only $50 million of a $75 million authorized enforcement appropriation and understaffing its fraud caseload; the Department faced no consequences when the bill died.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship split 87 Democrats and 21 Republicans among the 108 total, and the bill died without a floor vote, so there was no recorded vote to show a partisan split.

industries.industry: Savings and loan industry (individuals under investigation for fraud and embezzlement)
industries.note: The bill would have forced the Justice Department to investigate and prosecute more than 21,000 pending referrals on a deadline and pursue restitution, directly threatening suspects with liability for losses that fell on taxpayers. Its failure left enforcement running on the Department's slower timetable.

industries.industry: Savings and loan industry (institutional thrifts generally)
industries.note: Honest thrifts stood to gain from faster cleanup of fraud cases and a healthier deposit insurance fund, even as they faced closer scrutiny. The bill regulated conduct rather than imposing new fees.
